pairs.es: Which point on the diagram represents the earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: Point D — the single point where the distance circles from all three seismograph stations (A, B, C) intersect.

pairs.es: What is the name of the method shown for locating an earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: Triangulation — using the P-wave and S-wave arrival time difference at three seismograph stations to pinpoint the epicenter.

pairs.es: What does each circle drawn around a seismograph station represent?
pairs.en: The calculated distance from that station to the earthquake epicenter, determined by the time gap between P-wave and S-wave arrivals.

pairs.es: Points E, F, and G are where only two circles overlap. Why is the epicenter NOT at those points?
pairs.en: The epicenter must be where all three circles meet. E, F, and G are only intersections of two circles, so they are not confirmed by all three stations.

pairs.es: Why do you need at least three seismograph stations to locate an epicenter — why isn't one enough?
pairs.en: One station gives distance only (a circle of possible locations). Two stations narrow it to two points. A third station identifies the single correct point.

pairs.es: What two pieces of data does each seismograph station measure to calculate its circle's radius?
pairs.en: The arrival time of the P-wave and the arrival time of the S-wave. The larger the time gap between them, the farther the station is from the epicenter.

pairs.es: Why do the 'Shadow zone — No waves received' areas exist?
pairs.en: The liquid outer core blocks S-waves entirely and refracts (bends) P-waves away, creating zones on the opposite side of Earth where no seismic waves arrive.

pairs.es: At point B (bottom of the diagram), only one type of wave is received. Which type, and why?
pairs.en: Only P-waves. S-waves cannot travel through Earth's liquid outer core. P-waves can pass through liquids and still reach point B.

pairs.es: Point A is labeled 'P- and S-waves received here.' What does this tell you about point A's location?
pairs.en: Point A is close to the epicenter and outside the shadow zone. Both wave types can travel through the solid mantle to reach it without passing through the liquid outer core.

pairs.es: Which layer of Earth is responsible for creating the shadow zone?
pairs.en: The liquid outer core — it blocks S-waves completely and bends P-waves, leaving a zone on the far side of Earth where neither wave type arrives.

pairs.es: Why do the wave path arrows in the diagram curve instead of traveling in straight lines?
pairs.en: Waves refract (bend) as they pass through layers of different density. Denser layers speed up or slow down the waves, changing their direction.

pairs.es: How does the shadow zone provide evidence about Earth's interior?
pairs.en: The existence and location of the shadow zone proves Earth has a liquid outer core — only a liquid layer could block S-waves and bend P-waves enough to create that gap.

pairs.es: What does the star (✶) represent in Diagram 1?
pairs.en: The earthquake epicenter — the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus (the underground origin point of the earthquake).

pairs.es: Which labeled point(s) — A, B, C, or D — are located in the shadow zone?
pairs.en: Points B and C — they are on the far side of Earth from the epicenter, in the region where seismic waves are blocked or bent by the outer core.

pairs.es: Point A is near the epicenter. Which seismic waves would a seismograph at point A detect?
pairs.en: Both P-waves and S-waves — point A is close to the epicenter and outside the shadow zone, so both wave types reach it through the solid mantle.

pairs.es: Would a seismograph at point D detect seismic waves? Which types?
pairs.en: Yes — point D is on the same side of Earth as the epicenter and outside the shadow zone, so it receives both P-waves and S-waves.

pairs.es: Name the three layers labeled inside Earth on Diagram 1, from outermost to innermost.
pairs.en: Mantle → Outer core → Inner core. The mantle is solid rock; the outer core is liquid iron; the inner core is solid iron.

pairs.es: Why are the inner core and outer core shown as two separate layers?
pairs.en: They have different states: the outer core is liquid (blocks S-waves) and the inner core is solid (allows P-waves through). This difference in state affects wave behavior.

pairs.es: Which station (I, II, III, or IV) is closest to the earthquake epicenter, and how can you tell?
pairs.en: Station I — P-waves and S-waves arrive very close together, meaning a small time gap and therefore a shorter distance to the epicenter.

pairs.es: What does a larger time gap between P-wave and S-wave arrivals indicate?
pairs.en: The station is farther from the epicenter. Stations I → II → III show an increasing P-S gap, meaning each is progressively farther away.

pairs.es: Station IV shows only a P-wave arrival with no S-wave. What does this indicate about Station IV's location?
pairs.en: Station IV is in the shadow zone. S-waves cannot pass through Earth's liquid outer core, so they never arrive at Station IV.

pairs.es: Station I shows the largest wave amplitudes (biggest spikes). What does this tell you?
pairs.en: Station I is closest to the epicenter. More energy reaches nearby stations, causing stronger ground shaking and larger recorded amplitudes.

pairs.es: Among stations I, II, and III, which is farthest from the epicenter? How can you tell?
pairs.en: Station III — it has the largest gap between P-wave and S-wave arrival, meaning the most travel time difference and therefore the greatest distance.

pairs.es: How would you use the data from Stations I, II, and III together to locate the earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: Use the P-S time gap at each station to calculate distance. Draw a circle of that radius around each station on a map. The epicenter is where all three circles intersect (triangulation).

pairs.es: Seismograms record two distinct wave arrivals at most stations. What are those two arrivals, and which comes first?
pairs.en: P-waves (primary) arrive first — they are the fastest seismic waves. S-waves (secondary) arrive later — they travel slower and cannot pass through liquids.
